newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: West slams Milosevic over media crackdown.
newsitem.headline: West slams Milosevic over media crackdown.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic faced a growing chorus of criticism from the West as he tried to stifle opposition demonstrations against his nine-year rule.

The United States condemned a decision by the ruling Socialists to shut down an independent Belgrade radio station on Tuesday which had reported on daily street demonstrations that have attracted up to 100,000 people.

"This is a transparent effort to keep the Serbian public in the dark. It demonstrates the fundamental lack of respect, lack of regard the Serbian government has for democratic principles," a State Department spokesman said.
Washington was calling on its allies for a concerted international campaign against Belgrade's "anti-democratic" actions, spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

The closure of Radio B-92, coupled with an earlier police warning, indicated Milosevic was taking an increasingly tough line with the opposition. But the crackdown also risked fuelling the popular outrage behind the demonstrations.
A wave of street protests began more than two weeks ago after the opposition accused Milosevic's government of committing fraud to annul opposition victories in local polls earlier this month.
A spokesman for the Socialists shrugged off criticism from the United States and European powers over Milosevic's handling of the crisis.
"We regard the question of elections as an internal matter, and are behaving correspondingly," said Ivica Dacic, quoted by the state Tanjug news agency.
The opposition had always been allied with Serbia's critics and "had taken part in demonising this country", he said.
Some 80,000 students and opposition supporters marched through the streets of the capital again on Tuesday afternoon, joined by a group of U.S. congressmen.
Leaders of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition said closing the radio was a "desperate" act and warned that Milosevic might choose to use his police force to resolve the standoff.
The authorities have moved hundreds of police to Belgrade and other towns where the opposition has organised protests, but they have refrained from intervening so far.
Belgrade police, unlike on previous days, did little to direct traffic around the march and some commuters were frustrated with the congestion in the city centre.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader, vowed to carry on with the street protests until the New Year.
Western governments planned to convey their dismay to Serbian diplomats at a conference on Bosnia in London.
Despite strong words, Washington officials made clear there was no plan to push for a reimposition of a U.N. trade embargo on Belgrade.
U.S. action would be limited for now to maintaining an existing "outer wall" of American sanctions on Belgrade which blocks access to international financial institutions.
Five supreme court judges joined the opposition to Milosevic on Tuesday, accusing their colleagues of being politically subservient.

The judges' revolt, in letters to the opposition daily Nasa Borba (Our Struggle), was the first sign of a crack in the machinery of state over which Milosevic has maintained a tight grip during nine years of authoritarian government.
Serbian courts rubber-stamped Socialist claims of unspecified "irregularities" in the elections to clear the way for fresh ballots which the Socialists claimed they won.
With no sign of the demonstrations flagging, Milosevic was looking for a way out of the crisis to save face, diplomats said.
A city court was due to rule on a complaint from Zajedno which appealed against a municipal court's annulment of the opposition victory in Belgrade, local media reported.
